What do the original and redesigned aircraft look like in three dimensions?

Show code 
import aerosandbox.tools.pretty_plots as asbplt

redesign = constrained_redesign()
redesign_airplane = build_airplane(redesign["span"], redesign["chords"],
                                   redesign["twists"])

baseline_tip = SPAN / 2
redesign_tip = redesign["span"] / 2

# A drawing that let each aircraft fill its own panel would show no difference
# at all, so the shared limits below are the whole point of the figure.
assert redesign_tip > baseline_tip, "the redesign is not the longer wing"

Answer. Complete aircraft, one viewpoint, identical axis limits (Figure 1). The amber marks stand at the original’s wingtip, ±9.00 m; the redesign runs past them to ±9.95 m. Fuselage and tail were never design variables, so the whole visible difference is span, and the chord moved inboard to buy it.

WarningA rendering of the model, not a drawing of an aircraft

The surfaces come from the same parametric geometry the solver used. Airfoils, fuselage shape and tail are reconstructions, so this shows what was computed, not what was built.

Show code 
fig, axes = asbplt.figure3d(nrows=1, ncols=2, figsize=(7.2, 2.6),
                            computed_zorder=False)

half_width = redesign_tip * 1.03
for axis, airplane, name in [(axes[0], AIRPLANE, "Original"),
                             (axes[1], redesign_airplane, "Redesign")]:
    airplane.draw(backend="matplotlib", ax=axis, show=False,
                  use_preset_view_angle="left_isometric",
                  set_lims=False, set_equal=False)

    # Identical limits on both panels. Left to itself, draw() autoscales each
    # axis to its own aircraft, and both wings then fill their panel equally --
    # which would hide exactly the difference this entry exists to show.
    axis.set_xlim(-0.3, 7.0)
    axis.set_ylim(-half_width, half_width)
    axis.set_zlim(-0.7, 1.5)
    axis.set_box_aspect((7.3, 2 * half_width, 2.2))

    for side in (1, -1):
        axis.plot([2.0, 2.0], [side * baseline_tip] * 2, [-0.65, 0.75],
                  color="#b8860b", lw=1.6, zorder=10)

    axis.set_title(name, fontsize=9, pad=0)
    axis.set_axis_off()

fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.02, left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.96, bottom=0.02)
plt.show()
NoteThe method, as called 
def constrained_redesign(setup=None, subdivisions=1):
    """
    The redesign that cannot exploit the model, built the same way every time.

    Promoted once a third entry wanted it. The three constraints it applies are
    the ones the unconstrained optimum was found to be abusing: twist that
    oscillated to its bound, a tip chord that collapsed into a Reynolds regime
    the section data does not cover, and span bought without paying for the spar
    that carries it.

    The Reynolds floor is the BASELINE's own tip value, not a number invented
    for the purpose -- the design may not push the section anywhere the real
    aircraft does not already operate -- and it is returned alongside the design
    so an entry can assert the constraint actually bound.
    """
    setup = baseline_setup() if setup is None else setup
    floor = float(STATION_C[-1] * setup["speed"] / KINEMATIC_VISCOSITY)
    design = optimise(setup["limits"], washout_monotone=True,
                      reynolds_floor=floor, mass_model=True,
                      subdivisions=subdivisions)
    return {**design, "reynolds_floor": floor}
